options: A list of documents, each with its words
A map from each word to the list of documents that contain it
A copy of the table sorted by id
A cache of the last searches
why: It turns "document, then its words" round into "word, then its documents", like the index at the back of a book. A search reads the lists, not the documents.

q: Documents: 1 "red running shoes", 2 "blue running shirt", 3 "red red shirt", 4 "green hat". What does a search for "red shirt" give?
options: Documents 1, 2 and 3
Document 3 only (red twice and shirt once, score 3)
Documents 1 and 3
Nothing
why: red is in 1 and 3, shirt is in 2 and 3. Only document 3 is in both lists. Its score is red twice plus shirt once.

q: In the test with 200,000 rows, a GIN index helped a lot for a rare word and little for a word in 30% of rows. Why?
options: A common word has a very short list
A common word matches many rows, so most of the work is reading those rows
GIN indexes do not work for common words at all
The index is rebuilt on every search
why: A rare word was 29 ms with ILIKE and 0.2 ms with the index. A word in 30% of rows was 20.1 ms against 9.3 ms. An index helps most when few documents match.

q: The app saves a product in Postgres, then calls the search engine, which is down. The user sees "saved". What is wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing, the engine will find it later by itself
The two disagree for good (a dual write). Write an outbox row in the same transaction, and let a relay retry
Postgres must wait until the engine is up
The engine must be the only copy of the data
why: A crash between two writes leaves them different. The outbox is written in the same transaction as the data, so the change is not lost, and a relay retries until the indexer has it.

q: The indexer applied "upsert doc 1, version 2". Then "upsert doc 1, version 1" arrives late. What should it do?
options: Apply it, because it arrived last
Ignore it as stale, because its version is not newer
Apply it and delete version 2
Stop and raise an alarm
why: The indexer keeps the newest version it has seen for each id and applies only a bigger one. A late old change must not undo a newer one.

q: A user edits a product and searches one second later through a search engine such as Elasticsearch. Do they always find the new text?
options: Yes, search is always instant
Not always. A change shows after a refresh (about 1 second by default) plus any queue delay
Never, search engines cannot be updated
Only if the product has a version number
why: The Elastic docs say document changes are not visible to search immediately. Show the user's own change from the database and let the search catch up.
